records.place: Vila Nova de Gaia and Quinta de Vargellas, Porto, Douro

wine.name: Taylor's Vintage Port
wine.classification: Vintage, a special category of Port approved by the IVDP tasting chamber
wine.grapes: A field blend of Douro red grapes: Touriga Nacional and Touriga Franca at its core, with Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Tinto Cão and others.
wine.sites: Quinta de Vargellas in the Douro Superior, the backbone of the blend, with Quinta de Terra Feita in the Pinhão valley and, since 2000, a little of Quinta do Junco beside it, all on steep terraced schist.
wine.making: Grapes from the house's own quintas are trodden by foot in lagares, the granite ones of Vargellas among them, and grape spirit is added partway through fermentation to stop it and keep the wine sweet. The wine then matures in wood for a little under two years, about twenty months for the 2017, before bottling; the rest of its life is spent in bottle.
wine.glass: Violet, blackberry and cassis over graphite and liquorice; sweet and dense, held by firm, grippy tannin and a long, dry edge. Old bottles turn to dried fig, cedar and leather.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed when young; a strong declared year wants twenty years or more in bottle and keeps for decades beyond.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; stand the bottle upright for a day, then decant it off its crust; a small wine glass.

label.means: Port of one declared year, approved by the IVDP and bottled young to age in bottle.
The protected name of Port, the fortified wine of the Douro, in Portuguese.
The name the house uses in some markets, the United States among them, for the same Port.

records.table: Taylor's Vintage Port is the declared Port of a house founded in 1692, trodden by foot from its own quintas, Vargellas in the Douro Superior above all. Violet and blackberry sit on firm, grippy tannin, so give it decades and decant it off its crust.
records.story: Taylor's dates its start to 1692, when an English merchant of the Bearsley family came to Portugal, trading at first in the lean red wine of the Minho rather than Port. In 1744 the house bought its first property in the Douro, near Régua, remembered in its First Estate Port. Partners joined through the nineteenth century, and by the house's account it took the name Taylor, Fladgate & Yeatman in 1844. Between 1893 and 1896 it bought the three properties of Vargellas in the Douro Superior, two of them from the contractor who had built the railway along the river, and joined them into one quinta. Phylloxera had ruined the vines; a partner of the Yeatman family rebuilt the estate, and by 1908, as the house tells it, its wine was good enough for the Vintage blend. In 1974, in a time of political turmoil in Portugal, Taylor's bought Quinta de Terra Feita in the Pinhão valley, whose wine it had bought since the previous century. The house declares a Classic Vintage only in years it judges strong, announcing it by custom on 23 April of the second year; in other good years Vargellas is bottled alone. Taylor's stands for firm, slow Vintage Port, a wine to lay down for decades.

others.name: Quinta de Vargellas Vintage Port
others.note: The single quinta Vintage, from Vargellas grapes alone, bottled in years when no Classic Vintage is declared.

others.name: Quinta de Vargellas Vinha Velha
others.note: A small selection from the old vines of Vargellas, made only in rare years.

others.name: Taylor's First Estate
others.note: A Reserve Port named for the house's first Douro property, bought near Régua in 1744.

traps: A Classic Vintage is declared by the house in strong years; in good undeclared years Quinta de Vargellas is bottled alone, and it is Vintage Port all the same.
Taylor's and Taylor Fladgate are one house: the second name is the one the house uses in some markets, the United States among them.
Vintage Port spends under three years in wood and the rest of its life in bottle, so it throws a crust and must be decanted; a tawny does not.

cards.front: Taylor's Vintage Port: which quinta in the Douro Superior is the backbone of the blend?
cards.back: Quinta de Vargellas, bought between 1893 and 1896, with Terra Feita in the Pinhão valley beside it.

cards.back: 23 April, in the second year after the harvest.

questions.q: A guest asks how Taylor's makes its Vintage Port at the quintas. Which method does the house use?
opts: Treading by foot in lagares
Fermenting in new oak barrels
Ageing under flor in a solera
Heating the wine in a tank
questions.exp: Taylor's treads the grapes of its own quintas by foot in lagares and stops the fermentation with grape spirit; flor and soleras belong to sherry, and heated tanks to Madeira.

questions.q: In which years did Taylor's buy the properties of Vargellas, the quinta that gives the backbone of its Vintage Port?
questions.exp: The house bought the three Vargellas properties between 1893 and 1896 and joined them; 1744 brought its first Douro property near Régua, and 1974 Terra Feita.

sources.title: Taylor's: Quinta de Vargellas, the winery
Taylor's: Quinta de Terra Feita, the Taylor purchase

report: Every fact rests on the house's own pages read through search summaries (Our History, the Vargellas winery, the Terra Feita purchase, Quinta do Junco, the 2017 Vintage Port, the Vargellas single quinta page); Wikipedia's Taylor, Fladgate and Yeatman page was read beside them for 1692 and 1744.

The year the partners joined differs between accounts (Joseph Taylor in 1814, 1816 or 1826; John Fladgate in 1836 or 1837; the name fixed in 1838 by one account and 1844 by the house's), so the story names no partner's year and gives the house's 1844 as its own account.

The founder and the Yeatman partner who rebuilt Vargellas are described, not named, as no dates for them were found in two sources; Junco's share in the blend since 2000 is on the house's Quinta do Junco page, which is not in the list for want of room.
The library's region line has the first commercial LBV with the 1965 vintage released in 1970; it was not searched here and is left out of the record.
Living people met and kept out: the house's managing director and its head winemaker, both of the families that hold it; the read together agent may add their names to people.json.
Searches for this record: 7 of the group's 35, with 2 more on the IVDP's Vintage and tawny rules shared by the group.

wine.name: Graham's Vintage Port
wine.classification: Vintage, a special category of Port approved by the IVDP tasting chamber
wine.grapes: Touriga Franca and Touriga Nacional at its heart, with Sousão and grapes from old mixed vines, in shares that change with each declared year.
wine.sites: Quinta dos Malvedos above the river Tua, the house's first vineyard, bought in 1890, with Quinta do Tua, Quinta das Lages, Vila Velha and Vale de Malhadas, on the Douro's terraced schist.
wine.making: The grapes are trodden in the lagares of the house's winery at Malvedos, robotic ones built to copy the human foot since the 2000 vintage, with a share trodden by foot in some years, and grape spirit stops the fermentation. The wine spends about eighteen months in wooden vats at the house's lodge of 1890 in Vila Nova de Gaia, cooled by the sea air, and is bottled by the third year after the harvest, as the rules require.
wine.glass: Ripe plum, blackberry and violet over dark chocolate and liquorice, with a touch of eucalyptus; rich and sweet through the middle, gripped by firm, ripe tannin, with a long finish.
wine.ageing: Rich enough to tempt young, but a strong year needs fifteen to twenty years to open and goes on for decades after.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; stand it upright, then decant it off its crust an hour or so before pouring; a small wine glass.

label.means: Port of a single declared year, approved by the IVDP and bottled by the third year after the harvest.
The protected name of the fortified wine of the Douro, in Portuguese or in English.

records.table: Graham's Vintage Port comes from a house founded in 1820, and Quinta dos Malvedos above the Tua has been its heart since 1890. Rich and plummy, it needs years in bottle; decant it off its crust and pour it after dinner.
records.story: Two brothers of the Graham family were in the textile trade, and in 1820, as the house tells it, they accepted twenty seven barrels of Port in payment of a debt and so found themselves in the wine business. In 1882 a young Scot came out from Glasgow to work for the Grahams; his family, the Symingtons, became Port shippers in their own right. In 1890 the house bought its first vineyard, Quinta dos Malvedos, on the hill above the river Tua, and its vines became the cornerstone of Graham's Vintage Port; the lodge in Vila Nova de Gaia where the house ages its wines carries the same year in its name. In 1970 the young Scot's grandsons bought Graham's from the Graham family. With the 2000 vintage, by the house's account, its grapes were first trodden in robotic lagares built to copy the human foot, and its Vintage Port is made in the house's own winery at Malvedos. Graham's declares a Vintage only in years it judges strong; in good years that are not declared, Malvedos is bottled alone. For a sommelier it is the rich, plummy voice of the Symington family's Vintage Ports.

others.name: Graham's Quinta dos Malvedos Vintage Port
others.note: The single quinta Vintage, bottled in good years that are not declared.

others.name: Graham's 20 Year Old Tawny
others.note: A blend of wines of many years aged in seasoned casks at the lodge of 1890, with the character of twenty years in wood.

others.name: Graham's Six Grapes
others.note: A Reserve Ruby, sold ready to drink; often taken for a Vintage, which it is not.

traps: Quinta dos Malvedos on a label is a single quinta Vintage of an undeclared year, not Graham's declared Vintage Port.
Graham's was founded by the Graham brothers in 1820 and bought by the Symington family only in 1970, though a Symington first worked for the house in 1882.
Six Grapes is a Reserve Ruby ready to drink, not a Vintage Port.

cards.front: Graham's: how did two brothers in the textile trade enter the Port business in 1820?
cards.back: They accepted twenty seven barrels of Port in payment of a debt, as the house tells it.

cards.front: Which quinta above the Tua, bought in 1890, is the heart of Graham's Vintage Port?
cards.back: Quinta dos Malvedos, the house's first vineyard.

questions.q: A guest asks where Graham's Vintage Port spends its short time in wood before bottling. What is the answer?
opts: Wooden vats at the lodge of 1890 in Gaia
New French barrels at Quinta dos Malvedos
A solera of old butts in Jerez
Heated steel tanks at the quinta
questions.exp: Graham's ages all its wines at its lodge of 1890 in Vila Nova de Gaia, cooled by the sea; a Vintage spends about eighteen months in wooden vats there, not in new barrels at the quinta.

questions.q: In what year did the Symington family buy Graham's from the family that founded it?
questions.exp: The Symingtons bought Graham's in 1970; 1882 is when their forebear first came to Porto to work for the Grahams, and 1890 when the house bought Malvedos.

report: Dates and quintas rest on the house's own pages read through search summaries; the 1882 arrival from Glasgow is also in Wikipedia's Symington Family Estates page and a family memoir quoted by The Drinks Business.

The brothers and the young Scot of 1882 are described, not named with dates: no dates for William and John Graham were found, and the 1863 to 1939 commonly given for the Symington forebear was not confirmed by any source read.
The Symingtons bought Malvedos back after 1970: eleven years later by a house sheet, 1982 by Wikipedia; the record leaves the repurchase out.

The rich, plummy house style rests on a Tasting Panel report of a Symington tasting and a second taster's note; the library's contrast with Dow's drier finish was not confirmed by a source read and is left out.
Living people met and kept out: members of the Symington family who run the house and its winemakers (two Symingtons are already in people.json).
Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35, with the IVDP's Vintage rules shared by the group.

records.place: Above Pinhão in the Cima Corgo, Porto, Douro

wine.name: Quinta do Noval Nacional Vintage Port
wine.classification: Vintage, a special category of Port approved by the IVDP tasting chamber
wine.grapes: A field blend of many traditional Douro red varieties, planted together, every vine on its own ungrafted roots.
wine.sites: The Nacional parcel, a small plot at the heart of the Noval vineyard on the terraced schist above Pinhão. Its vines stand on their own roots rather than American rootstock and are replanted the same way, so they are not pre-phylloxera survivors.
wine.making: The grapes are trodden by foot in the quinta's stone lagares, exactly as for the rest of the Noval vineyard, and grape spirit stops the fermentation. The wine then spends about eighteen months in large casks of oak and chestnut in the estate's temperature controlled cellars in the Douro before bottling.
wine.glass: Violet, blackberry and black cherry over liquorice and dark chocolate, deeper and denser than the estate's other Vintage Port; sweet yet gripped by tight, firm tannin. Old bottles turn to dried fig, cedar and tobacco.
wine.ageing: Slower to open than Noval's own Vintage Port; the house gives it a drinking window of five to a hundred years, and strong years are kept for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; rest the bottle upright for a day, decant it gently off its crust shortly before serving; a small wine glass.

label.means: The ungrafted parcel inside Quinta do Noval; the house reads the name as Portuguese vines in Portuguese soil.
A wine estate in Portugal; here the Noval estate above Pinhão.
Port of one declared year, bottled young to age in bottle; Nacional is declared on its own.

records.table: Quinta do Noval Nacional is Vintage Port from a small parcel of ungrafted vines at the heart of the Noval estate above Pinhão, trodden by foot and declared only in exceptional years. Dense and slow, it asks for long cellaring and a careful decant.
records.story: The name Noval first appears in the land registers in 1715. After phylloxera had ruined the vineyard, a Port shipper bought the estate in 1894 and replanted it, and his son in law went on to widen its narrow old terraces so that the vines could make better use of the land and the sun. Inside the vineyard a small plot was planted on its own roots, ungrafted; the house says its name, Nacional, means Portuguese vines in Portuguese soil, with no foreign rootstock. Noval made its name in 1931, as the house tells it, by declaring both a Vintage Port and a Nacional in a year when most shippers did not, with the world in depression and the large 1927 vintage unsold. In 1981 a fire destroyed the archives, offices and part of the cellars in Vila Nova de Gaia, and the stocks were later moved to a temperature controlled cellar on the quinta. The family that had held Noval since 1894 sold it in 1993, and it joined AXA Millésimes. Nacional is declared on its own judgement: in 1996 it was declared when Noval was not, and in 2007 Noval was declared without it. For a sommelier it is the Douro's lesson in what ungrafted vines can give.

others.name: Quinta do Noval Vintage Port
others.note: The estate's Vintage from the rest of the vineyard, declared on its own judgement apart from the Nacional.

others.name: Quinta do Noval Colheita
others.note: A tawny from a single harvest, aged long in cask before bottling.

traps: Nacional is a parcel inside Quinta do Noval, not a separate quinta, and it is declared apart from Noval's own Vintage Port.
Ungrafted is not pre-phylloxera: the Nacional vines grow on their own roots and are replanted that way.
Nacional names the ungrafted parcel, not the grape Touriga Nacional; the wine is a field blend.

cards.front: Quinta do Noval Nacional: what sets its vines apart from the rest of the estate?
cards.back: They grow on their own roots, ungrafted, with no American rootstock, and are replanted that way, so they are not pre-phylloxera vines.

cards.front: Name a year when Quinta do Noval declared its Nacional but not its own Vintage Port.
cards.back: 1996; in 2007 the reverse, Noval declared without the Nacional.

questions.q: A guest asks what makes Quinta do Noval Nacional different from Noval's own Vintage Port. Which answer is right?
opts: Its vines grow ungrafted on their own roots
It is aged for decades in small casks
It is made from Touriga Nacional alone
It comes from bought grapes upriver
questions.exp: Nacional comes from a small parcel of ungrafted vines inside the estate; it is a field blend of many varieties, and its name does not refer to Touriga Nacional.

questions.q: Quinta do Noval made its name by declaring a Vintage and a Nacional in a year when most shippers held back. Which year?
questions.exp: Noval declared both in 1931, in the depression and with the large 1927 vintage unsold, when most houses did not declare; 1927 was the year the trade had declared widely.

sources.title: Quinta do Noval: The particularity of our Nacional Vintage Port
Quinta do Noval: Nacional Vintage Port

report: Every date rests on the house's own pages and timeline read through search summaries; the importer's page (Vintus) and Winerist's article on Nacional agree that no pre-phylloxera vines remain although the vines were never grafted.

The shipper of 1894 (António José da Silva) and his son in law (Luiz Vasconcelos Porto) are described rather than named, as no dates for either were found; their grandsons of the van Zeller family who sold in 1993 are not named either.

The house's founding year of 1715 is the year the name first appears in the land registers, not a founding; the library gives 1715 as founded and the record keeps it, telling it in the story as the first record.
The 1931 Nacional as the first Nacional bottled was not confirmed and is not claimed.
One summary of the house's page says phylloxera never reached the parcel; the record does not say so, as the library and two other sources have the vines replanted on their own roots.
The library's line that Noval is owned by AXA Millésimes is volatile; the record says it joined AXA Millésimes in 1993.
Living people met and kept out: the managing director already in people.json and the van Zeller family members.

records.place: Quinta da Leda, Douro Superior, Douro DOC, Portugal

wine.name: Barca Velha
wine.grapes: Touriga Franca and Touriga Nacional at its heart, with Tinta Roriz and other Douro grapes; the shares change with each declared year.
wine.sites: Quinta da Leda in the Douro Superior gives the greater part, with high parcels nearby; the first vintages were made at Quinta do Vale Meão, a Ferreira family estate in the same subregion.
wine.making: The wine is aged for about a year and a half in French oak barrels, most of them new, then rests for years in bottle while the house watches it. Only then does the winemaking team decide whether the year is Barca Velha or Reserva Especial, so a vintage reaches the market eight or nine years after the harvest.
wine.glass: Cedar and cigar box over blackcurrant, sour cherry and plum; savoury and restrained rather than ripe, with fine, firm tannin, fresh acidity and a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Released when the house judges it ready to begin drinking, eight or nine years after the harvest, it goes on gaining for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant an hour ahead, an old bottle gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Old boat in Portuguese; the name is printed only in declared years.
The appellation of the valley's unfortified wines; Port carries the separate name Porto.
The house name of Ferreira's unfortified Douro wines, after Dona Antónia Ferreira's nickname.

records.table: Barca Velha is Casa Ferreirinha's unfortified Douro red, first made in 1952 and declared only in exceptional years after long rest in bottle. Savoury, cedar framed and fresh, it showed that Port's grapes could make a dry red to keep; decant it.
records.story: Dona Antónia Adelaide Ferreira (1811 to 1896), widowed at thirty three, took charge of the Ferreira house, founded in 1751, and at her death left more than two dozen estates in the Douro; the region called her Ferreirinha, and the poor called her their mother. The dry wine that carries her nickname began more than half a century after her death. Fernando Nicolau de Almeida (1913 to 1998), whose father was the house's technical director, wanted a Douro red made with the care given to Vintage Port. At Quinta do Vale Meão, in the heat of the Douro Superior, he built a double walled vessel packed with ice brought by lorry from Matosinhos, near Porto, and in 1952 declared his first Barca Velha, selling it only in 1960, when he judged it ready to begin drinking. The harvest of 1960 gave the first Reserva Especial, the name for strong years judged short of Barca Velha. The Ferreira house joined Sogrape in 1987, and in later decades Quinta da Leda in the Douro Superior became the main source of the blend. The 2015, released after nine years, was the twenty first Barca Velha since 1952. For a sommelier it marks where the Douro's fine dry reds begin.

others.name: Casa Ferreirinha Reserva Especial
others.note: From strong years the team judges closer to Reserva Especial than Barca Velha; first made in 1960.

others.name: Quinta da Leda
others.note: The single estate red of the Douro Superior quinta that gives most of Barca Velha.

traps: Barca Velha is not made every year: strong years that fall short may be released as Reserva Especial, and many years give neither.
Ferreirinha is the nickname of Dona Antónia Ferreira, a person, not a place.
Barca Velha is an unfortified red of the Douro DOC, not a Port, though it comes from the same grapes.

cards.front: Barca Velha: who made the first vintage, in 1952, and at which quinta?
cards.back: Fernando Nicolau de Almeida, at Quinta do Vale Meão in the Douro Superior.

cards.front: What becomes of a Casa Ferreirinha vintage that is strong but not judged Barca Velha?
cards.back: It may be released as Reserva Especial, a name first used for the 1960.

questions.q: A guest orders Barca Velha expecting a sweet Port to finish the meal. What do you tell them?
opts: It is a dry, unfortified Douro red
It is a Vintage Port from one quinta
It is a tawny Port aged in cask
It is a sweet red of dried grapes
questions.exp: Barca Velha is an unfortified red of the Douro DOC, dry and savoury; it shares Port's grapes but is never fortified, so it is not a Vintage Port.

questions.q: The first Barca Velha was made in 1952. In which year did it first go on sale?
questions.exp: Fernando Nicolau de Almeida held his 1952 back for eight years and sold it in 1960, when he judged it ready; 1987 is the year the Ferreira house joined Sogrape.

sources.title: Sogrape: Porto Ferreira, a secular tradition
Sogrape: Barca-Velha 2015, the twenty first vintage
Sogrape: Casa Ferreirinha presents Reserva Especial 2017
The Drinks Business: Casa Ferreirinha Barca Velha 2015 released

report: Fernando Nicolau de Almeida's dates, his father's post, Vale Meão, the ice from Matosinhos and the release of the 1952 in 1960 rest on Wikipedia and Observador's special on Barca Velha (https://observador.pt/especiais/barca-velha-ou-a-historia-de-como-nascem-os-grandes-vinhos/), with Infopédia agreeing on the dates; Observador is left out of sources for want of room.
The purpose of the ice, to cool the fermentation in the heat, is implied rather than stated, as the summaries read did not say it in so many words.
The barrel time rests on two release notes (sixteen months in new French oak for the 2008, eighteen months mostly new for the 2015); early vintages saw Portuguese oak by one account only, left out.

The library gives the grapes as led by Tinta Roriz and Touriga Franca; Sogrape names Touriga Franca and Touriga Nacional first, and one account has Tinta Roriz dominant in early years such as 1982 and Sousão added in 2015, so the record gives the two Tourigas at the heart and Tinta Roriz beside them.

The founding year 1751 is the Ferreira house's, as Sogrape gives it; Casa Ferreirinha is the name of its unfortified wines, and no source read dated that name. The year 1987 for Sogrape rests on Sogrape's own article on the Porto Ferreira Vintage 2018.
The meaning of the name Barca Velha beyond its translation, old boat, was given by one source only (sailing boats that carried young Port downriver) and is left out.
Living people met and kept out: the head winemaker since 2007 and his predecessor, both named on Sogrape's pages.
Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35.

records.place: Vila Nova de Gaia, Porto, Douro

wine.name: Sandeman 20 Year Old Tawny Port
wine.classification: Tawny with an indication of age, a special category of Port approved by the IVDP
wine.grapes: Touriga Franca and Tinta Roriz above all, with Tinta Barroca, Tinta Amarela and Tinto Cão.
wine.sites: Grapes from vineyards along the Douro, blended and aged downriver in the house's lodges at Vila Nova de Gaia, across the river from Porto.
wine.making: The grapes are hand picked, destemmed and crushed, then fermented on their skins at a controlled temperature until grape spirit is added to stop the fermentation and keep the sugar. The wines age for many years in oak casks in the lodges, and wines of several ages are blended to show the character of twenty years in wood.
wine.glass: Amber with a red edge; walnut, toasted almond, dried fig and orange peel over caramel and a hint of cinnamon, sweet and silky, lifted by fresh acidity, with a long, nutty finish.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink when bottled, with no need to lay it down; once opened, the house advises finishing it within two or three months.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, lightly chilled; no need to decant, though a little air helps; a small white wine glass.

label.means: An indication of age: the blend shows the character of twenty years in cask, not the age of every wine.
Port aged in wood until its colour fades towards amber and its fruit turns to nuts and caramel.
Port's protected name in Portuguese; an aged tawny's label also gives its bottling year.

records.table: Sandeman 20 Year Old Tawny comes from the house of the caped Don, founded in London in 1790: Port aged for many years in oak casks in its lodges at Vila Nova de Gaia. Walnut, orange peel and caramel; pour it lightly chilled, without decanting.
records.story: In 1790 a young Scot of the Sandeman family, twenty five years old and the son of a cabinetmaker, borrowed from his father to set up as a wine merchant in London. From the start the house dealt in Port and sherry, the two fortified wines of Iberia, and at first it traded not from offices of its own but from Tom's Coffee House in Birchin Lane, as merchants then did. The founder bought lodges at Vila Nova de Gaia to hold its Port before shipment, and by the middle of the nineteenth century, by the house's account, it was shipping fine old tawny aged in their cool cellars. In 1928 an artist at a printing firm drew the Don, a silhouette in the black cape of a Portuguese student and a Spanish hat, one for Port and one for sherry. The family ran the firm until 1952, when it became a public company; Seagram took it over in 1980, by the house's account, and in 2002 it joined Sogrape, the Portuguese wine group. For a sommelier the 20 Year Old shows what decades in cask do to Port: fruit turned to walnut, orange peel and caramel, poured cool and without a decanter.

others.name: Sandeman Quinta do Seixo Vintage Port

traps: Twenty years on a tawny label is an indication of age, the character of the blend, not the age of every wine in it.
Sandeman was founded in London by a Scot, not in Porto; its Port ages in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia across the river.
A 20 Year Old Tawny is ready when bottled and throws no crust; a Vintage Port does, and is decanted.

cards.front: Sandeman: what does the Don wear, and what does each piece stand for?
cards.back: A Portuguese student's black cape for Port and a Spanish hat for sherry.

cards.front: On a Sandeman 20 Year Old Tawny, what does the age statement promise?
cards.back: The character of twenty years in cask, from a blend of wines of several ages; the label also gives the bottling year.

questions.q: A guest asks whether Sandeman 20 Year Old Tawny means every drop is twenty years old. What is the answer?
opts: No: the blend shows twenty years' character
Yes: every wine in it is from one harvest
Yes: it spent twenty years in bottle
No: it spent twenty years under flor
questions.exp: An indication of age describes the character of a blend of wines of several ages aged in wood; a tawny from a single harvest would be a Colheita, not a 20 Year Old.

questions.q: In what year was the Sandeman Don, the caped silhouette on the label, first drawn?
questions.exp: The Don was drawn in 1928 at a printer's studio; 1790 is the founding in London, and 1952 the year the family firm became a public company.

Grape to Glass: Sandeman 20 Years Tawny Port sheet

report: The house's history, the Don and the 20 Year Old's making and service rest on Sandeman's own pages read through search summaries; the one fetch of sandeman.com was refused and not retried.

The founder is described rather than named: his birth in 1765 follows from the house's page (twenty five in 1790) and a wine glossary, but his death in 1841 was in one source only; Perth as his home is in a partner's page and a Wikipedia mirror, so the story leaves it out.
